# Introduction

A classifier can be accurate for the wrong reason: instead of the feature that
defines a class, it may exploit an easier predictive shortcut that works on
the training data and on standard benchmarks but fails when conditions change
[@geirhos2020]. The cue is a spurious correlation, and relying on it is called
shortcut learning (also known as the Clever Hans effect). A dermoscopy network
for melanoma recognition gave higher melanoma scores to lesions with gentian
violet surgical skin markings: its specificity
fell from 84.1% for unmarked to 45.8% for marked lesions, and heat maps linked
the markings to the increase [@winkler2019].

We inject an artificial colour shortcut into MNIST and ask three questions.
(1) How strongly does a network rely on it, depending on the architecture and
the strength of the correlation? (2) Can mitigation at the data level or at
the loss level remove the reliance? (3) Can explainability methods reveal it?

# Literature Review

Geirhos et al. showed that ImageNet-trained CNNs depend heavily on texture
while humans rely mainly on shape, and that training on Stylized-ImageNet
shifts a network towards shape and improves robustness [@geirhos2019].

Mitigation can act on the data or on the training objective. Idrissi et al.
show that simply balancing classes and groups, by subsampling or reweighting,
matches state-of-the-art worst-group-accuracy methods while training faster and
needing no additional hyperparameters [@idrissi2022]. Counterfactually
augmented data, introduced for text, are documents that annotators revise so
that the label flips with minimal changes, which can make models less
sensitive to spurious patterns [@kaushik2020]. Just Train Twice needs no group
labels: it upsamples the examples that a first model fits poorly and retrains
[@liu2021]. To inspect what a model uses, we apply Grad-CAM [@selvaraju2016],
Integrated Gradients [@sundararajan2017] and LIME [@ribeiro2016].

# Dataset Preparation

We use MNIST (60,000 training and 10,000 test digits) and paint each digit in
one of ten colours, one per class. In the biased training set a digit receives
the colour of its class with probability $p$ and a random colour otherwise. A
random colour is correct one time in ten, so the colour matches the class in
$p + (1-p)/10$ of the images: 55%, 91% and 99.1% for $p = 0.5$, $0.9$ and
$0.99$. A clean training set, the grayscale digit repeated in three channels,
serves as control.

Each model is evaluated on four test sets built from the same 10,000 test
digits, which differ only in colour: *aligned* (the colour of the digit's
class), *clean* (no colour), *random* (a random colour) and *conflicting* (the
colour of class $(y+1) \bmod 10$). We report accuracy on each, the *shortcut
rate* (the share of conflicting images predicted as the colour's digit) and
the *gap* (accuracy on aligned minus accuracy on conflicting images); a large
gap means the model follows the colour.

# Model Training and Evaluation

We compare a fully connected network (MLP, 103,982 parameters) with a small
CNN (106,154 parameters); the MLP has one hidden layer of 44 units so that
both models have almost the same size. The CNN has two blocks of convolution
($3 \times 3$), ReLU and max pooling with 16 and 32 filters, followed by linear
layers $1568 \to 64 \to 10$. All 39 trainings use one shared loop
(cross-entropy, Adam with learning rate $10^{-3}$, batch size 128, 5 epochs)
and seeds 0, 1 and 2; we report mean ± standard deviation over the seeds.

| model | training | $p$ | aligned | conflicting | shortcut rate | gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MLP | clean | -- | 95.2 ± 0.6 | 96.3 ± 0.2 | 0.3 ± 0.1 | -1.1 ± 0.5 |
| MLP | biased | 0.9 | 99.0 ± 0.0 | 81.6 ± 1.3 | 6.4 ± 0.6 | 17.4 ± 1.3 |
| CNN | clean | -- | 96.3 ± 0.4 | 97.2 ± 0.9 | 0.2 ± 0.1 | -1.0 ± 1.3 |
| CNN | biased | 0.5 | 99.1 ± 0.1 | 97.3 ± 0.1 | 0.6 ± 0.1 | 1.8 ± 0.1 |
| CNN | biased | 0.9 | 99.6 ± 0.1 | 93.2 ± 0.3 | 2.7 ± 0.3 | 6.4 ± 0.2 |
| CNN | biased | 0.99 | 99.9 ± 0.0 | 58.0 ± 4.6 | 28.3 ± 5.7 | 41.9 ± 4.6 |

: Test accuracy (%) and shortcut measures without mitigation, mean ± std over
3 seeds. {#tbl-baseline}

Biased models reach 99--100% on aligned images, higher than clean-trained
models, so a normal test set hides the shortcut (@tbl-baseline). Models
trained on clean data show no gap, so the gap is caused by the injected
colour. At equal size the MLP has a larger gap (17.4 points) than the CNN
(6.4); a possible reason, which we did not test, is that convolutional filters
respond to local shape. The strength of the correlation matters most: the
CNN's gap grows from 1.8 points at $p = 0.5$ to 41.9 at $p = 0.99$, where only
about 540 training images have a conflicting colour.

# Data mitigation

We test two mitigations that change only the training data. The model, loss,
optimiser, epochs and test sets stay as in the baseline, so differences in
accuracy can be attributed to the data (@tbl-mitigation).

*Augmentation* paints each digit with a new random colour every time it is
read, always starting from the original grayscale digit: recolouring an
already coloured digit could keep a brightness that depends on the old colour
and therefore on the class, a hidden shortcut. The colour then matches the
label only by chance (about 10%), and the method does not depend on $p$. It
follows the idea of randomising the shortcut, as Stylized-ImageNet does for
texture [@geirhos2019].

*Rebalancing* adds conflicting copies, the same digit painted in a colour that
is never its class, until the colour matches the label in 50% of the images.
This adds about 49,000 ($p = 0.9$) or 59,000 ($p = 0.99$) images, so the
training set grows to about 109,000 and 119,000 images. This is related to data
balancing [@idrissi2022] and counterfactual augmentation [@kaushik2020].

# Model mitigation

*Reweighting* keeps the data and changes the loss: samples whose colour
differs from the label get weight 10, all others weight 1, and the loss is the
mean of the weighted per-sample cross-entropy. It needs the shortcut label of
every training image but creates no new images and keeps 60,000 samples.

| $p$ | method | aligned | clean | conflicting | gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.9 | none | 99.6 ± 0.1 | 93.1 ± 1.8 | 93.2 ± 0.3 | 6.4 ± 0.2 |
| 0.9 | augmentation | 98.3 ± 0.2 | 98.3 ± 0.2 | 98.3 ± 0.2 | 0.0 ± 0.0 |
| 0.9 | rebalancing | 99.3 ± 0.1 | 98.5 ± 0.1 | 98.0 ± 0.2 | 1.2 ± 0.1 |
| 0.9 | reweighting | 98.4 ± 0.2 | 96.6 ± 0.2 | 95.5 ± 0.3 | 2.9 ± 0.4 |
| 0.99 | none | 99.9 ± 0.0 | 67.2 ± 5.7 | 58.0 ± 4.6 | 41.9 ± 4.6 |
| 0.99 | augmentation | 98.3 ± 0.2 | 98.3 ± 0.2 | 98.3 ± 0.2 | 0.0 ± 0.0 |
| 0.99 | rebalancing | 99.2 ± 0.1 | 98.5 ± 0.1 | 98.3 ± 0.2 | 1.0 ± 0.1 |
| 0.99 | reweighting | 99.4 ± 0.0 | 83.6 ± 5.1 | 80.8 ± 1.3 | 18.6 ± 1.3 |

: All mitigations, test accuracy (%), mean ± std over 3 seeds. The gap is
averaged per seed, so it can differ by 0.1 from the rounded difference.
{#tbl-mitigation}

Augmentation and rebalancing reach about 98--99% on all test sets at both
values of $p$. Augmentation removes the gap completely but loses accuracy on aligned images
(98.3% against 99.6--99.9%), because colour is no longer a useful cue;
rebalancing leaves a gap of about 1 point, perhaps because the training
correlation is still 0.5, which we did not test. Reweighting helps less: at
$p = 0.9$ it raises conflicting accuracy from 93.2% to 95.5%, and at
$p = 0.99$ by 22.8 points to 80.8%, with a gap of 18.6 points remaining. One
reason is visible in the weights: at $p = 0.99$ only 0.9% of the training
images are conflicting, so with weight 10 they carry about 8.3% of the total
weight (49.7% at $p = 0.9$). Equal total weight would need a weight of about
110, which we did not try, so this comparison holds for the fixed weight only.

Further caveats: rebalancing uses about twice as many images and gradient
steps, so part of its gain may come from more data; augmentation needs the
original digits and the knowledge that colour is the shortcut, rarely available
for real shortcuts; and with three seeds and at most 0.5 points between them
we do not rank augmentation and rebalancing.

# Explainable AI

Grad-CAM turns the gradients flowing into the last convolutional layer into a
coarse heatmap [@selvaraju2016], Integrated Gradients accumulates gradients
along a path from a baseline input to score every input feature
[@sundararajan2017], and LIME fits a simple model around a single prediction
[@ribeiro2016]. We applied Grad-CAM and Integrated Gradients to the baseline
and the three mitigated models. 

# Conclusion

A normal test set hides the shortcut: biased models reach 99--100% on aligned
images but fall to 58.0% on conflicting images at $p = 0.99$, and the reliance
grows with the strength of the correlation and differs between architectures.
Mitigation on the data removed the gap almost completely (at most 1.2 points),
and reweighting with a fixed weight reduced it from 41.9 to 18.6 points. These
results come from one dataset, one known synthetic shortcut, two small
architectures and 3 seeds; unknown shortcuts, as in most real applications,
are a harder problem that our experiments do not address.
